strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in current LRMs - the inability to appropriately admit ignorance
Provides clear empirical evidence of two pathological reasoning patterns (last-minute guessing, second-thought spiraling) with compelling pilot study
Offers valuable insight that current RL training paradigms fail to reward refusal, explaining root cause of overconfidence
Comprehensive and thorough experimental evaluation including ablations, OOD generalization tests, pass@k analysis, and mathematical reasoning preservation
Significant empirical improvements in reliability (39.33% → 61.48%) while maintaining accuracy
Well-structured two-stage training approach combining SFT and GRPO with clear mechanistic insights
Good reproducibility with detailed experimental details, hyperparameters, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited to small models (7-8B parameters), all distilled versions; no experiments on models ≥13B or full-scale LRMs, severely limiting applicability claims
Missing comparisons with recent factual alignment methods (FLAME, DPO-based approaches, RLKF, R-tuning); weak baselines (ICL, ICL-IDK, proprietary Distill)
Heavy reliance on GPT-4 for knowledge labeling and reasoning trace construction introduces quality dependencies and sustainability concerns
Evaluation restricted to factual QA with verifiable answers; explicitly cannot handle open-ended tasks that are common in real-world LRM applications
SFT stage exhibits fundamental accuracy-truthfulness trade-off (Figure 4) suggesting suboptimal pipeline design; GRPO needed to fix SFT's failures without clear justification for two-stage approach
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multi-run results; all results appear to be single runs
Knowledge labeling via sampling strategy has no error sensitivity analysis; borderline cases not addressed
Reasoning patterns identified informally; third pattern discovered in appendix suggests incomplete taxonomy; no quantitative breakdown of failure contribution by pattern
Algorithm 1 lacks details on alternative candidate selection (yj, ej); reward function values (rc > rw > rs) not ablated or justified
Mechanism explanation incomplete - unclear how/why BARREL training accesses internal knowledge boundary representations identified by prior work

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: LRM hallucinations and overconfidence
Clear identification of specific pathological reasoning patterns with empirical evidence (Figure 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets, models, metrics, and generalization tests (OOD, pass@k)
Significant empirical improvements in reliability metric (39.33% → 61.48%)
Solid ablation studies, particularly on SFT trade-offs and reward design necessity
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: combines existing techniques (sampling-based labeling, SFT, GRPO) without fundamental innovations; rule-based rewards are simplistic compared to modern learned reward models

Critical unaddressed dependence on GPT-4 for trace generation: circular dependency between model labeling and training, unclear how much improvement is due to distillation from GPT-4 vs. the BARREL framework itself, limits reproducibility
Knowledge labeling via sampling lacks quality analysis: no study of false positives/negatives, label sensitivity, or computational costs of K×L model runs
Evaluation scope limited to factual QA with verifiable answers: no comparison with other refusal training baselines, missing human evaluation, string matching evaluation is imperfect (88% accuracy)
Unresolved accuracy-truthfulness trade-off: final accuracy (40.7%) barely exceeds baseline (38.43%); main improvement comes from refusing unknowns rather than improving knowledge or reasoning

Overclaimed novelty in contributions: prior work (Zhang et al. 2024a, Cheng et al. 2024, Xu et al. 2024) already addresses training models to refuse; the paper conflates method novelty with conceptual novelty
Incomplete ablations: no SFT-only or GRPO-only baselines, unclear necessity of two-stage training, no continuous sensitivity analysis of reward magnitudes

Rule-based reward design (Eq. 4) overly simplified: specific values lack justification, Figure 5 uses only binary ablation, no learned reward model comparison, sensitivity to reward magnitudes unexplored
Scale and generalization concerns: evaluation limited to small models (8B/7B), SimpleQA OOD test shows 3% accuracy suggesting potential over-refusal, no cross-dataset generalization tests
Algorithm 1 underspecified: unclear how alternative candidates and evidence are actually obtained, reasoning trace quality and diversity not analyzed, no sensitivity study of trace variations

strengths: Important and timely problem addressing factual reliability of LRMs with clear dual-aspect framing (knowing vs. telling)
Well-motivated problem identification through concrete pathological reasoning patterns with empirical support (Figure 2)
Strong empirical results showing substantial reliability improvement (39.33% to 61.48%, ~22% absolute gain) while maintaining accuracy
Comprehensive experimental design with multiple datasets, thorough ablations, pass@k analysis, and OOD generalization testing
Novel insight about medium-level rewards being essential for refusal—identifies fundamental gap in current RL paradigms
Clear presentation with excellent visual communication and well-structured methodology
Good reproducibility practices with detailed training details and promised code availability
weaknesses: Limited to small models (7-8B parameters) due to computational constraints—unclear if results generalize to larger models where this method may be needed most
Narrow evaluation scope restricted to verifiable factual QA; no evaluation on open-ended questions, opinions, or creative tasks
Strong dependency on external tools: sampling-based knowledge labeling (requires ground truth and multiple inferences) and GPT-4 for reasoning trace generation with no quality analysis
Weak baselines—limited comparison with other uncertainty/calibration methods from related work; 'Distill' baseline appears underdeveloped; no comparison with confidence-based thresholding
Reward design underspecified: three-level rewards lack justification, actual values not reported, limited sensitivity analysis beyond Figure 5
Fundamental accuracy-refusal trade-off in SFT (Figure 4) remains unresolved; GRPO partially addresses it but indirectly; final accuracy (40.7%) remains modest for practical use
Missing systematic failure analysis: no quantification of when method fails (false negatives/positives), which question types are problematic, or failure mode characterization
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple seed runs despite small test set sizes (1000 questions per dataset)
Reliability metric formulation (Rel. = ans·Truth + (1-ans)·Acc) appears ad-hoc with insufficient justification for specific weighting
Limited comparison with recent refusal-training methods (R-tuning, RLKF) mentioned in related work but not empirically compared

strengths: Clear identification of important problem: Factual overthinking in LRMs and two well-motivated failure modes (last-minute guessing, second-thought spiraling)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets, models, ablations, OOD tests, pass@k analysis, seed variability, and stability analysis across appendices
Substantial and consistent empirical improvements: ~22 percentage point reliability gains across multiple models (DeepSeek-R1 variants, Qwen3-8B)
Thorough justification of design choices: Demonstrates necessity of both SFT and GRPO stages; shows medium-level refusal rewards are crucial (Figure 6)
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, data construction prompts, code/data release promised, appendix with randomness analysis
Well-structured two-stage training addresses identified failure modes: SFT teaches refusal patterns, GRPO optimizes accuracy-refusal trade-off
Strong qualitative analysis: Concrete examples (Table 2, appendices) effectively show transformation from pathological to reliable reasoning
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: Evaluation restricted to factual QA with verifiable answers; no evaluation on open-ended generation, instruction-following, math, or other domains

Weak knowledge labeling methodology: Binary known/unknown distinction cannot distinguish genuine confusion from ignorance; acknowledged mislabeling in SFT stage with no quantification of impact or sensitivity analysis

Heavy dependence on GPT-4 data: SFT training data synthetically generated by GPT-4; unclear how much improvement is from BARREL framework vs. from training on high-quality reasoning traces; limited ablation (Table 3 shows both strategies converge after GRPO)
Reward design appears empirically tuned: Specific values (rc=1, rs=-0.5, rw=-1) lack principled justification; no systematic ablation of reward values; raises generalization concerns
Sampling instability: ~20% inconsistency rate across 4 samples (Appendix K) for borderline queries; abstractly different decisions across runs undermine reliability
Limited theoretical understanding: Purely empirical paper with minimal mechanistic insight into why approach works; Appendix O provides only brief reference to prior work

Moderate absolute accuracy: 40.7% accuracy with 29.7% refusal rate; unclear if performance-reliability trade-off is optimal; different applications need different operating points but fixed rs commits to one threshold
Fixed uncertainty threshold: Cannot adapt to different risk tolerances without retraining; acknowledged in Appendix Q as limitation but left as future work

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine unreliability in LRMs with clear empirical examples
Thorough and comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple datasets, models, and detailed ablations (trade-off analysis, pass@k, OOD generalization, stability analysis)
Substantial quantitative improvements (39.33% → 61.48% reliability on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, consistent across multiple models)
Interesting empirical observation of 'factual overthinking' phenomenon with clear visualization in Figure 2
Transparent acknowledgment of limitations with extensive supplementary analysis and hyperparameter details supporting reproducibility
Well-organized presentation with clear examples and good visualization of reasoning patterns (Tables 2, 10, 11)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing methods (sampling-based labeling from Gekhman et al. 2024, standard SFT, existing GRPO algorithm); reward design (rc > rs > rw) is straightforward rather than principled

Fundamental unresolved flaw in knowledge labeling: sampling-based approach fails when model oscillates between options—precisely where refusal is most needed; GRPO only partially mitigates, leaving mislabeled SFT data

Critically narrow scope restricted to factual QA: authors acknowledge (Appendix P) that 'overthinking' doesn't characterize unreliability in instruction-following or reasoning tasks; no evidence for broader applicability despite claims about 'System 2 LRMs'

No human evaluation of refusal appropriateness or calibration quality; only string matching evaluation with GPT proxy; critical question unanswered: are refusals actually well-calibrated for user trust?
Insufficient model scale: only tested on models up to 8B parameters; authors acknowledge limited computing resources; unclear if approach scales to larger/state-of-the-art reasoning models
Pass@k trade-off inadequately addressed: Figure 5 shows GRPO reduces absolute pass@k accuracy compared to SFT; claim of 'similar trend' obscures actual sacrifice of sampling-based accuracy
Data construction quality concerns: GPT-4-generated traces lack human validation; only one rewriting ablation (Table 3); unclear if quality is consistent across domains or GPT-4 biases present

Missing critical technical details: Algorithm 1 vaguely specifies 'alternative candidates with poor evidence'; Eq. 4 doesn't specify how 'valid rejection phrase' is detected—implementation crucial for reproducibility
High residual inconsistency: ~20% inconsistency rate (Appendix K) means for 1 in 5 borderline cases model's refusal decision varies across samples; acknowledged but not adequately solved

Missing human evaluation and important comparisons: no human evaluation of calibration; limited comparison to recent uncertainty quantification, confidence calibration, or retrieval-augmented baselines; confidence methods treated as strawman
Arbitrary reward design: rc=1, rs=-0.5, rw=-1 values not justified; Figure 6 shows sensitivity but doesn't explore design space or how to configure for different risk tolerances

SFT-GRPO trade-off mechanism unclear: Figure 4 shows SFT forces accuracy-truthfulness trade-off; GRPO recovery mechanism (whether just RL seeing both correct/incorrect samples) not adequately analyzed
Limited statistical rigor: only 5 random seeds (Table 12); no confidence intervals or significance tests; unclear which improvements are statistically significant

Overstated scope in framing: title and abstract claim broad 'Reliable LRMs' and 'System 2' capabilities, but only factual QA demonstrated; no evaluation on reasoning, instruction-following, or open-ended tasks

strengths: Identifies and clearly articulates the 'factual overthinking' phenomenon in reasoning models, with consistent empirical evidence across multiple models (Figure 2)
Substantial empirical improvements in reliability (>20% gains from 39.33% to 61.48%) while maintaining comparable accuracy, demonstrated across multiple models and datasets

Comprehensive evaluation including multiple datasets, extensive ablations (reward values, data ratios, SFT strategies), OOD generalization (SimpleQA, unanswerable questions), seed variability analysis, and pass@k analysis
Well-motivated three-component framework with clear logic and practical applicability; the insight about medium-level rewards highlights a genuine gap in current RL paradigms
Thorough analysis with concrete examples (Table 2), detailed reasoning trace examples, and extensive appendices; reproducibility well-supported with detailed hyperparameters and promised code release
Novel two-stage approach combining SFT for seeding refusal behaviors with GRPO for calibrated abstention, specifically targeted to reasoning model pathologies
weaknesses: Limited scope of evaluation: primarily small models (7B-8B); unclear scalability to larger models or non-reasoning LMs; applicability only demonstrated on factual QA domain with verifiable answers

Imperfect knowledge labeling: sampling strategy is itself a proxy that cannot distinguish genuine confusion from ignorance; authors acknowledge 'certain proportion of mislabeled data in the SFT stage'
Heavy dependency on GPT-4 for SFT data construction raises reproducibility concerns; limited ablation of data construction choices (only Constructing vs. Rewriting comparison)
Unresolved calibration issues: ~20% inconsistency rate across samples (Appendix K); for borderline questions, decisions remain sensitive to sampling noise
Domain generalization severely limited: framework tailored to factual QA; acknowledged that 'overthinking' not pathological for instruction-following or mathematics; inapplicable to open-ended tasks

Incomplete theoretical understanding: why medium-level reward works better lacks principled explanation; reward values (rc=1, rs=-0.5, rw=-1) appear empirically driven; acknowledged that fixed reward 'limits flexibility for scenarios requiring different risk tolerances'
Inconsistent accuracy trade-offs: NQ-Open shows accuracy drops to 20.9% (BARREL) vs 31.1% (Vanilla GRPO), suggesting model becomes overly conservative for some datasets
Limited baseline comparisons: post-hoc baselines (Verbal Confidence, Probing) are relatively simple; insufficient comparison with recent factual alignment methods (RLKF, Self-alignment, etc.)
Computational cost of training not discussed; failure case analysis absent; question-type specific improvements not investigated
